About: the curl as the circulation round a small loop divided by its area, for a rigidly rotating fluid and the field of a thick wire

About this simulation

On screen
Looking down the axis, with x and y from −3.5a to 3.5a: faint circles about the axis at 0.5a to 3.0a, field arrows every 0.5a whose lengths are proportional to the field (the scale is in the note under the view), for the wire its cross-section of radius a with the current coming out of the page, and the paddle wheel inside its loop: outer arc blue, inner arc red, radial sides grey, arrowheads anticlockwise. The inset plots the circulation divided by the area against s: teal dots for the fluid, orange dots for the wire.
Controls
Field: the rotating fluid or the straight wire; switching keeps the wheel where it is. Drag the wheel anywhere in the view, or use the x and y sliders; its distance s from the axis stays between 0.5a and 3.0a (steps of 0.05a when dragged). Every move adds a dot to the inset.
Measured
Each arc contributes its radius times the field on it times the angle 0.4a/s between the radial sides; the radial sides contribute nothing. Circulations are in ωa² (fluid) or μ₀I/2π (wire), divided by the loop's area 0.16a².
Readouts
In the sidebar under Controls: the wheel's distance s, which way it turns and the time per turn, the two arcs' contributions and the circulation, and circulation/area. The wheel turns at half the circulation/area, on one scale for both fields (2 units = ω = π/2 rad/s). For the wire the wheel is a picture of the curl of B, not a real object that B would turn.
The Paddle Wheel and the Curl
✦Teach me
Looking down on the planefield arrows, loop and paddle wheel · inset: circulation/area against s

Guided Inquiry

1 · A wheel in the rotating fluid

Choose the rotating fluid and leave the wheel at s = 2.0a on the positive x-axis. Before watching the wheel, predict what it does.

2 · Near and far

Keep the rotating fluid. You will drag the wheel in to s = 0.5a and then out to s = 3.0a. Before you do, predict how its rate of turning changes.

3 · Round a straight wire

Switch to the straight wire and drag the wheel to s = 2.0a. Before watching the wheel, predict what it does.

4 · The two arcs

Keep the straight wire with the wheel at s = 2.0a; afterwards you will drag it out to s = 3.0a. Before looking at the readouts for the two arcs, predict how their contributions to the circulation compare at the two distances.

5 · Inside the wire

Keep the straight wire and drag the wheel into the wire, to s = 0.5a. Before watching the wheel, predict what it does.

6 · What you found

The curl is the circulation round a small loop divided by its area: a small paddle wheel turns at half of it.

A rigidly rotating fluid has curl 2ω everywhere, so the wheel turns at ω wherever it is put.

Outside the wire, B falls as 1/s and the two arcs cancel: circular field lines, but no curl. Inside, B grows as s and the curl is μ0J. The curl of B is nonzero only where current flows: ∇×B = μ0J.

The Physics

The Paddle Wheel and the Curl · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

A small paddle wheel sits at a distance s from an axis, in a field whose lines run in circles about it. The sim offers two such fields, the flow of a rigidly rotating fluid and the magnetic field of a straight wire of radius a, and turns the wheel to match the circulation round its small loop.

What you'll learn

  • How the sim measures a field's tendency to turn the wheel.
  • Whether the wheel turns in each field, and how fast.
  • How that changes with the distance s.
  • What differs inside the wire and outside it.
The two fields, with the small loop at s = 2a. Arrow scales differ between the panels, as in the sim.

What's on screen

  • Main view: looking down the axis, x and y from −3.5a to 3.5a, with faint circles at s = 0.5a to 3.0a and field arrows every 0.5a.
  • Outer arc of the wheel's loop, blue, and inner arc, red. The radial sides are grey.
  • Wire: its cross-section of radius a, current out of the page.
  • Inset: circulation/area against s, with teal dots for the fluid and orange dots for the wire.
See itLook at the sim at its opening values. Watch for: the loop round the wheel with its blue outer arc and red inner arc, and the arc rows in the Readouts.

Fixed: the loop spans s − 0.2a to s + 0.2a, with the radial sides 0.4a/s apart, so its area is 0.16a². Circulations are in ωa² for the fluid and in μ0I/2π for the wire, and circulation/area is in ω or in μ0I/2πa². Both fields share one scale for the wheel: a reading of 2 is ω = π/2 rad/s.

03

Circulation per area measures how hard a field turns the wheel

For a loop small enough that the field barely changes across it, the circulation round the loop divided by its area is the component of the curl along the loop's normal. The wheel's loop is a small piece of a circle, so the sim adds up its four sides.

(∇ × B)·n̂ ≈ ∮ B·dℓ / area

The curl as circulation per unit area; notes section 5.3, The Curl.
The loop, enlarged. The outer arc runs anticlockwise and the inner arc the other way, so the circulation is their sum.

Each arc contributes its radius times the field on it times the angle 0.4a/s between the radial sides. The radial sides run across the field and add nothing. The wheel turns at half the circulation/area, and on the sim's scale a reading of 2 is ω = π/2 rad/s, one turn every 4.0 s.

See itLeave the fluid at s = 2.0a. Watch for: Circulation equal to Outer arc plus Inner arc, and Circulation / area equal to that sum divided by 0.16.
04

In the rotating fluid the wheel turns at ω

For a body rotating with angular velocity ω the velocity is v = ω × r, so round the axis vφ = ωs. Its curl is 2ω, the same at every point.

∇ × (ω × r) = 2ω

The curl of a rigidly rotating body; notes section 5.3, The Curl.

At s = 2.0a the outer arc gives +0.968 and the inner arc −0.648, in units of ωa². The circulation is 0.320 ωa², and over the area 0.16a² that is 2.000 ω. The wheel turns anticlockwise, the same way as the fluid, once every 4.0 s.

Key idea. Circulation per area is 2ω, so a small wheel in a rigidly rotating fluid turns at ω.
See itChoose the rotating fluid and leave the wheel at s = 2.0a. Watch for: Outer arc +0.968, Inner arc −0.648, Circulation / area 2.000, Turning anticlockwise and Time per turn 4.0 s.
05

The wheel turns at the same rate at every distance

The fluid moves faster further out, so the outer arc contributes more. But the inner arc takes away just as much more, and the circulation does not change. From s = 0.5a to 3.0a the outer arc grows from +0.392 to +1.365 and the inner arc goes from −0.072 to −1.045.

The two arcs in the fluid at three distances. Both grow with s, and their sum stays 0.320.

Each time the circulation stays 0.320 ωa², so circulation/area stays 2.000 ω and the wheel still turns once every 4.0 s. In cylindrical form the curl is (1/s) d(s vφ)/ds, and with svφ = ωs² that is 2ω at every s.

See itKeep the rotating fluid and put the wheel at s = 0.5a. Watch for: Outer arc +0.392 and Inner arc −0.072, yet Circulation / area still 2.000.
See itNow put the wheel at s = 3.0a. Watch for: Outer arc +1.365 and Inner arc −1.045, with Time per turn still 4.0 s.
06

Round a straight wire the two arcs cancel and the wheel stays still

Outside a straight wire the field is Bφ = μ0I/2πs, so its lines are circles but it weakens as 1/s. An arc's length grows as s while the field on it falls as 1/s, so the radius times the field is the same on both arcs.

The two arcs round the wire at three distances. They are equal and opposite each time, so their sum is 0.

At s = 2.0a the arcs give +0.200 and −0.200, in units of μ0I/2π, so the circulation is 0.000 and the wheel does not turn. At s = 3.0a they give +0.133 and −0.133, smaller but still equal and opposite.

Key idea. Circles are not enough for a curl: the weakening of the field with distance compensates for the curving of its lines.
See itSwitch to the straight wire and put the wheel at s = 2.0a. Watch for: Outer arc +0.200, Inner arc −0.200 and Circulation / area 0.000.
See itNow put the wheel at s = 3.0a. Watch for: Outer arc +0.133 and Inner arc −0.133, still cancelling.
07

Inside the wire the wheel turns again

Inside a wire of radius a with uniform current the field is B = (μ0I/2πa²)(−y, x, 0), the same form as v = ω × r with ω = μ0I/2πa². Its curl is μ0J, which is not zero where the current flows.

∇ × B = μ0J

Ampère's law in differential form; notes (5.45).

At s = 0.5a the sim reads 2.000, the same as the fluid's 2ω on this sim's scale, and the wheel turns anticlockwise once every 4.0 s. While the loop straddles the surface, from s = 0.8a to 1.2a, the reading falls from 2 to 0. At s = 1.0a it is 0.900.

Circulation/area against s, computed from the sim's loop. The fluid stays at 2, while the wire reads 2 inside, falls across its surface and reads 0 outside.
field s

These sliders move the sim too. The values come from the sim's own loop model.

See itSwitch to the wire and put the wheel at s = 0.5a. Watch for: Circulation / area 2.000 and Turning anticlockwise.
See itNow put the wheel at s = 1.0a. Watch for: Circulation / area falling to 0.900 and Time per turn rising to 8.9 s.
08

Where it matters

  • Stokes' theorem and Ampère's law. A circle round the wire has circulation μ0I although the curl is zero everywhere outside the wire. Every surface bounded by the circle is crossed by the wire, where the curl is μ0J, so that is where the circulation comes from (notes (5.43)).
  • Static fields. The electrostatic field has ∇ × E = 0 everywhere, so a wheel in any static E would never turn, while ∇ × B = μ0J (notes (5.46)). The wire's field also shows why a conservative force needs a region with no holes.
  • Where the model stops. The loop is a finite 0.4a wide, so near the wire's surface the sim reports a loop average, not the curl at a point. For the wire the wheel is a picture of the curl of B, not a real object that B would turn.
09

Summary

In one line. The wheel responds to the circulation round its small loop divided by the loop's area, the curl of the field at that place.

Common mix-ups

  • "Circular field lines mean a curl." Outside the wire the arcs give +0.200 and −0.200, and the curl is 0.
  • "The fluid is faster further out, so the wheel spins faster there." The inner arc takes away more too. At 3.0a the arcs give 1.365 and −1.045, still 0.320.
  • "The stronger field on the near side turns the wheel backwards." The near arc is shorter by exactly the factor by which its field is stronger.
  • "The wire's field has no curl anywhere." Inside the wire it is μ0J, and the sim reads 2.000 at s = 0.5a.

Things to try on your own

  • In the fluid, put the wheel at (0, 2), (−2, 0) and (0, −2) and compare each reading with the one at (2, 0).
  • On the wire, drag the wheel in from s = 1.5a and watch circulation/area rise from 0 to 2.
